entities.name: monotheism in Islam
entities.label: Idea
entities.summary:
Monotheism in Islam, known as *Tawhid* (تَوْحِيد), represents the absolute and indivisible oneness of God (Allah) and stands as the foundational theological concept of the Islamic faith, established in the Arabian Peninsula during the 7th century CE by Prophet Muhammad. This uncompromising assertion of a singular divine entity, devoid of partners, offspring, or any form of association (*shirk*), fundamentally shaped the nascent Muslim community (*umma*) and provided the ideological bedrock for a civilization that would span continents and millennia. Its significance lies in its role as the primary doctrine uniting diverse peoples under a common creed, distinguishing Islam from prevailing polytheistic practices and even other monotheistic traditions of its time.

The core of *Tawhid* dictates that God is unique, eternal, omnipotent, and omniscient, the sole creator and sustainer of the universe, deserving of all worship. This principle manifested practically in the rejection of idolatry, the dismantling of pagan shrines like those in Mecca, and the establishment of a new socio-political order centered on submission to God's will. The Quran, revealed to Muhammad starting around 610 CE, serves as the primary textual source articulating these principles, emphasizing God's transcendence (*tanzih*) and immanence (*tashbih*) while strictly forbidding any anthropomorphic or polytheistic interpretations. This theological clarity provided a powerful unifying force for the early Muslim conquests and subsequent state-building efforts.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Monotheism in Islam, known as *Tawhid*, fundamentally reshaped the religious and political landscape of the 7th-century Arabian Peninsula and subsequently became the core doctrine for a global civilization that continues to influence nearly two billion people today, impacting art, philosophy, law, and social structures across continents.
